title: Microburst latency profiles and max_tokens simulation
content:
Context and motivation:

This is a working note for an exploratory eval that tries to capture how short, high-concurrency bursts (microbursts) interact with: batching policies, prefix/KV cache hit rates, and max_tokens caps during model onboarding. Goal: understand tail-latency risk and cost blow-ups that are not visible in steady-state throughput tests.

Why this matters:
- Real customer traffic often includes microbursts (search spikes, UI autocompletes, multi-tab retries) that break assumptions from long-running throughput experiments.
- Models with large variance in generation length (e.g., open-chat-type) can push sudden token spikes that increase latency and cost nonlinearly.
- Onboarding evaluators and serve configs need safety margins and fallback logic; this doc captures initial sims and recommended guardrails.

Experiment summary (high level):
- Workload: 10k simulated sessions over 15 minutes with embedded microbursts (5s windows where QPS spikes 5x–20x).
- Models: rwi-7b-quant (example onboarding candidate), rwi-14b-compat (baseline), and a smaller 3B proxy for cost-limited runs.
content_continued:
NOTE: agents.md requires flat JSON — I split content into two keys to keep lines readable.

Environment and setup:
- Infra: Dedicated GPU pool (A100x2 equivalent), single-region sim to isolate runtime scheduling effects.
- Serving runtime flags: continuous_batching=true, max_batch_size=64/128 (swept), batching_timeout_ms=10/50/100 (swept).
- Caching: prefix cache simulated at 0%, 30%, 60% hit rates. KV cache warm vs cold scenarios included.
- max_tokens sweep: client-level caps at {64, 128, 256, 512}. Also an adaptive cap scenario (cap = median_length*1.5).
- Prompt set: 1k prompts sampled from product chat and autocomplete buckets; mix of short (avg 12 tokens) and long (avg 120 tokens).

Metrics collected:
- Per-request: p50, p95, p99 latency (server-side), generation tokens emitted, failure/retry counts, queue-time, batch-size at execution.
- Aggregate: tokens/sec and tokens/hour, inferred cost per 1M tokens (model-specific), tail-latency frequency (requests > 1s, >2s).
- System events: scheduling preemption, model-switch/fallback activations.

Key observations (early, exploratory):
1) Microburst amplification: when batching_timeout_ms is high (100ms) microbursts create very large batch sizes that reduce cost-per-token but spike p99 latency catastrophically for short-request flows (short prompts waiting behind long generations).
2) Cache hysteresis: prefix cache at 60% reduces average latency but introduces variance — cache-miss requests (cold keys) get batched with warm keys, increasing their p99 more than the mean suggests.
3) max_tokens nonlinearity: moving cap from 128 to 256 during microbursts increased median tokens emitted by ~40% for the long-prompt subset, but increased p99 latency for short prompts by ~2.3x due to queueing/backpressure.
4) Adaptive caps can limit worst-case token growth but need robust prompt-length predictors; naive median-based cap still lets long-tail cases through and adds operational complexity.
5) Small-model fallback: automatically routing overflow to a cheaper 3B proxy reduced p99 latency for short prompts but introduced quality regressions on some prompt classes — need per-prompt quality checks before fallback.

Anecdotal trace (on a spike):
- t=0s: 150 concurrent requests for short prompts arrive in 5s window; batching_timeout_ms=50ms, max_batch_size=128.
- scheduler accumulates batches of 90–120; 30% of those were long-prompt requests (avg expected gen=300 tokens) — long gens drove per-device execution for 1.4–2.8s, short prompts waiting experienced 1.2–1.7s queue delays.
- cache hit-rate dropped mid-spike due to tail keys, increasing compute by ~18%.

Practical takeaways / recommended guardrails for onboarding configs:
- Conservative defaults: for hosted/Dedicated onboarding, set batching_timeout_ms=20ms and max_batch_size=64 as a starting safety profile for multi-tenant traffic with unknown distributions.
- Auto-fallback policy: implement a short-prompt detector (heuristic: prompt_token_count < 32 && intent=complete) that triggers fast-path routing to low-latency slices or small-model proxies under burst detection.
- max_tokens limits: enforce soft max_tokens per-tenant (e.g., 256) with a graduated grace policy (first N requests per minute allowed higher) to prevent single-user floods from expanding queue lengths.
- Observability: add per-request tags for "cache_hit_origin" and "batch_wait_ms" to the telemetry so we can attribute tail spikes to batching vs model execution time.
- Sim harness: expand sim to include multi-region fallbacks and cross-region routing latencies — microbursts often coincide with regional failovers.

Open questions and TODOs (notes-to-self):
- Q: Can we derive a cheap classifier that predicts generation length from prompt tokens + top-level metadata with >90% precision to enable better adaptive caps? TODO: run small classification experiment (Diego).
- Q: How do preemption policies interact with KV cache retention? If preempted work evicts useful KV, we lose cache benefits. TODO: link with infra/serving to validate preemption behavior (JIRA-ML-789).
- TODO: add cost model that factors in tail-latency penalties (e.g., SLA credits). Make a decision tree for when to sacrifice cost for latency under different customer tiers.
- TODO: export sample traces to Confluence page CONFLUENCE-12345 and annotate with flame graphs.

Quality regression notes:
- When testing small-model fallback we saw coherent hallucination increase on multi-step prompts (approx +6% F1 drop on eval set). Need to pair fallback with a rapid rerank/quality-check stage where possible.

Appendix: quick experiment matrix (compact):
- sweep dimensions: batching_timeout_ms {10,20,50,100}, max_batch_size {32,64,128}, cache_hit {0,30,60}, max_tokens {64,128,256,512}, burst_multiplier {5x,10x,20x}.
- target outputs: p99 < 700ms for short prompts under 10x burst for production tier; cost delta < 2x vs steady-state.

Links / refs:
- Sim harness code: https://github.com/redwood-inference/pr/456
- Follow-up ticket: JIRA-ML-789
- Confluence trace collection: CONFLUENCE-12345

Notes to reviewers:
- This is exploratory; numbers are from early sims and will change when we include multi-region routing and real-network jitter. Please flag any missing workload types that you'd like included (e.g., streaming small token increments from many concurrent clients).

Signed-off: Aisha
